title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
The goal of this lab was to assemble the E155 development board, confirm that both the FPGA and MCU boards work, and write SystemVerilog code to drive three LEDs and a seven-segment display. The design reads four DIP switches s[3:0] and produces:

led[0]: the XOR of s[1] and s[0]
led[1]: the AND of s[3] and s[2]
led[2]: a 2.4 Hz blink derived from the on-chip 48 MHz oscillator
seg[6:0]: hexadecimal digit 0–F selected by s[3:0]

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
The goal of this lab was to assemble the E155 development board, confirm that both the FPGA and MCU boards work, and write SystemVerilog code to drive three LEDs and a seven-segment display. The design reads four DIP switches s[3:0] and produces:

led[0]: the XOR of s[1] and s[0]
led[1]: the AND of s[3] and s[2]
led[2]: a 2.4 Hz blink derived from the on-chip 48 MHz oscillator
seg[6:0]: hexadecimal digit 0–F selected by s[3:0]

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
The design is split into four modules so some of the modules are reusable in later labs:

lab1_az.sv: top level module that instantiates the internal oscillator, led controller, and a switch-to-7-segment decoder, and drives three leds that represent the binary encoding of a hex number inputted by a switch.
led_controller.sv: instantiates the counter, outputs a 2.4 Hz blink signal from a 48 MHz clock.
counter.sv: a reusable counter that accepts parameters WIDTH and MAX_COUNT, and counts from 0 to MAX_COUNT-1 when enabled and wraps back to 0 when MAX_COUNT is reached.
seven_segment_decoder.sv: a reusable, combinational decoder that maps the switch input to its respective 7-segment display format.







NoteHow did we get 2.4 Hz?





For the counter, we have set MAX_COUNT = \(10,000,000\). This determines what the counter counts up to and therefore the output frequency, which in our case will also be the frequency at which led[2] blinks at. Because the on-chip oscillator oscillates at \(48\) MHz, and since we toggles led[2] half way through each count cycle, the blink frequency will be \(48\) MHz \(÷\) \(10,000,000\) cycles \(÷\) \(2 = 2.4\) Hz.



Each submodule has its own stim/assert testbench:

seven_segment_decoder_tb.sv exercies the decoder over all 16 input combinations.
counter_tb.sv checks the counter module for correct reset, enable, and max count behaviors.
led_controller_tb.sv checks the blinking led for correct reset, enable, and max count behaviors.
lab1_az_tb.sv checks that the submodules are wired together correctly and that the switch-to-LED logic matches the truth tables.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository.

Block Diagram



Figure 1: Block diagram of the SystemVerilog design.


The block diagram in Figure 1 demonstrates the overall architecture of the design The top-level module lab1_az includes three submodules: the high-speed oscillator block (HSOSC), the led controller module (led_controller), and the 7 segment decoder (seven_segment_decoder). The led controller includes the counter module (counter). The assign logic for two of the three output LEDs are shown with the XOR and AND logic gates.


Schematic



Figure 2: Schematic of the UPduino to the seven-segment display physical circuit.


Figure 2 shows the physical layout of the design. Internal 100 k \(\Omega\) pullup resistors were used to ensure the active low reset pin and the switches were not floating. This value was given by the lab instruction. Each of the 7 output segments were connected using a 150 \(\Omega\) current-limiting resistor to ensure the output current did not exceed the safety range of ~8 mA.






NoteHow did we get 150 \(\Omega\)?





From the 7-segment display datasheet, we obtained that the forward voltage per segment is typically \(2\) V. We know that the common anode is connected to \(3.3\) V, making the voltage drop across the resistor-LED segment combo \(3.3 - 2 = 1.3\) V. Using Ohm’s law and plugging in \(I = 8\) mA, we obtain an optimal resistor value of \(1.3\) V \(÷\) \(8\) mA \(= 162.5\) \(\Omega\). Since we don’t have that resistor value in lab, we will use \(150\) \(\Omega\) instead. Double checking, \(150\) \(\Omega\) with a \(1.3\) V voltage drop gives a current of \(8.67\) mA, which is still safe.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Results and Discussion

Testbench Simulation



Figure 3: A screenshot of a QuestaSim simulation for the 7 segment display.


Figure 3 shows a screenshot of the Questa simulation of the 7 segement decoder module. We tested across all 16 possible input combinations, as demonstrated in the second signal in the screenshot (s), with their respective output captured by the third signal in the screenshot (seg). All tests pass with no errors.


Other testbenches




Figure 4: A screenshot of a QuestaSim simulation for the top level design.


Figure 4 shows a screenshot of the Questa simulation of the lab1_az top level module. As the top signal CLKHF shows, the on-chip high-speed oscillator is generating a clock signal. All tests pass with no errors.



Figure 5: A screenshot of a QuestaSim simulation for the led controller.


Figure 5 shows a screenshot of the Questa simulation of the led controller module. All tests pass with no errors



Figure 6: A screenshot of a QuestaSim simulation for the counter.


Figure 6 shows a screenshot of the Questa simulation of the counter module. All tests pass with no errors.

The design met all intended design objectives.


Hardware
All prescribed tasks are accomplished. On hardware, all 16 switch positions were stepped through to confirm the displayed digit, and the LED truth tables and blink rate were verified. Both the LED and the 7-segment display changes instantly when the switch input is changed.



Figure 7: Picture of the LEDs and 7-segment display when output is 7.


As shown in Figure 7, when the switch is 0111 (hexadecimal 7), the 7-segment display correctly displays 7. And since s[0] ^ s[1] is 0, s[2] & s[3] is 0, neither of led[0] and led[1] are on. Led[2] is on since it is always blinking.


Another test case




Figure 8: Picture of the LEDs and 7-segment display when output is d.


As shown in Figure 8, when the switch is 1101 (hexadecimal D), the 7-segment display correctly displays d (lower-case to differentiate against 0). And since s[0] ^ s[1] is 1, s[2] & s[3] is 1, both led[0] and led[1] are on. Led[2] is also on since it is always blinking.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Conclusion
The design successfully controlled 3 LEDs and a 7-segment display using a 4-bit switch input and the on-board high speed oscillator. The displays were all very successful. I spent a total of 20 hours working on this lab.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display and Keypad Scanning
text:
The goal of this lab was to use time multiplexing to share one expensive hardware resource across two jobs, and to interrogate a matrix keypad by scanning it one row at a time. The design reads two independent 4-bit switch inputs s0[3:0] and s1[3:0], reads the four keypad columns col[3:0], and produces:

seg[6:0]: a single shared cathode bus, driven by one seven-segment decoder that alternates between the two digits
pnp[1:0]: one-hot anode enables that turn on exactly one display at a time through 2N3906 PNP transistors
row[3:0]: a rotating one-hot scan pattern driven onto the keypad rows through 2N3904 NPN transistors wired as open-collector outputs
led[3:0]: the inverted keypad columns, so that pressing a key blinks the LED for that column

Because a single decoder and a single set of segment pins serve both digits, the display costs 9 FPGA pins instead of the 14 that two independent decoders would need.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display and Keypad Scanning
text:
The goal of this lab was to use time multiplexing to share one expensive hardware resource across two jobs, and to interrogate a matrix keypad by scanning it one row at a time. The design reads two independent 4-bit switch inputs s0[3:0] and s1[3:0], reads the four keypad columns col[3:0], and produces:

seg[6:0]: a single shared cathode bus, driven by one seven-segment decoder that alternates between the two digits
pnp[1:0]: one-hot anode enables that turn on exactly one display at a time through 2N3906 PNP transistors
row[3:0]: a rotating one-hot scan pattern driven onto the keypad rows through 2N3904 NPN transistors wired as open-collector outputs
led[3:0]: the inverted keypad columns, so that pressing a key blinks the LED for that column

Because a single decoder and a single set of segment pins serve both digits, the display costs 9 FPGA pins instead of the 14 that two independent decoders would need.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display and Keypad Scanning
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
The design is split into five modules, two of which are reused unchanged from lab 1:

lab2_az.sv: top level module. It instantiates the internal oscillator (HSOSC), the time multiplexer (time_mux), the shared decoder (seven_segment_decoder), and the keypad row scanner (keypad_scanner), and contains a single assign statement that passes the keypad columns back out to the LEDs.
time_mux.sv: a 2:1 multiplexer in front of the shared decoder. A counter divides the 48 MHz clock; the first half of each count period selects s1 and the second half selects s0, and the matching anode enable in pnp[1:0] is asserted so that only the digit whose data is currently on the segment bus is lit.
keypad_scanner.sv: the row scanner. A counter provides the state, and four assign statements convert the count into the rotating one-hot pattern 1000 → 0100 → 0010 → 0001. The module is both resettable and enable-able, and it contains nothing other than the counter instance and the output assigns.
counter.sv: Counter from lab 1.
seven_segment_decoder.sv: Seven segement decoder from lab 1.

Per the simulation specifications, counter and seven_segment_decoder were not re-simulated, since both were verified with their own testbenches in lab 1 and neither was modified. The two new pieces of the design each have their own self-checking stim/assert testbench:

keypad_scanner_tb.sv walks the scanner through all four output transitions (including the wrap from 0001 back to 1000), checks that the output holds steady for a full row period rather than changing early, and checks the enable and reset features: the scanner freezes while enable is low, picks up where it left off when enable returns, and jumps back to 1000 when reset is asserted mid-scan.
lab2_az_tb.sv exercises the top module. It models the keypad inside the testbench by driving col from the current row pattern and a set of simulated key presses, so the design under test sees the same behavior it would on the bench. It checks that reset selects a known digit, that each digit is held for exactly half the refresh period and then swaps, that the two digits follow their own switch inputs independently, and that the LED path lights the correct LED for the row currently being scanned. The multiple-keypress case is tested explicitly: three keys are held at once, two of them sharing a column, and each lights its LED only while its own row is being driven.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display and Keypad Scanning
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository.

Block Diagram



Figure 1: Block diagram of the SystemVerilog design. Angela Zheng, 9/14/2026


The block diagram in Figure 1 shows the overall architecture of the design. The top-level module lab2_az contains four submodules: the high-speed oscillator block (HSOSC), the time multiplexer (time_mux), the shared seven-segment decoder (seven_segment_decoder), and the keypad row scanner (keypad_scanner). Both time_mux and keypad_scanner contain their own parametrized instance of the counter module. The single 4-bit net s_eff (s effective) carries the multiplexer output into the one decoder instance, which is what makes the decoder shared rather than duplicated, and the inverter on the col path is the only bare logic in the top module.


Schematic



Figure 2: Schematic of the UPduino and the dual seven-segment display, and the keypad. Angela Zheng, 9/14/2026


Figure 2 shows the physical layout of the dual seven-segment display design. Internal 100 k \(\Omega\) pullup resistors were used to ensure the active low reset pin and the switches were not floating. Each pair of the 7 output segments were connected using a 100 \(\Omega\) current-limiting resistor to ensure the FPGA output current did not exceed the safety range of ~8 mA.



Figure 3: Schematic of the UPduino and the keypad. Angela Zheng, 9/14/2026


Figure 3 shows the physical layout of the keypad design. Internal 100 k \(\Omega\) pullup resistors were used to ensure the active low reset pin and the column pins were not floating. Each column is pulled up using a 390 \(\Omega\) pull-up resistor, and each row are connected using a 330 \(\Omega\) current-limiting resistor to ensure the FPGA output current did not exceed the safety range of ~8 mA.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display and Keypad Scanning
text:
Results and Discussion

Testbench Simulation



Figure 5: A screenshot of a QuestaSim simulation for the keypad row scanner


Figure 3 shows the Questa simulation of keypad_scanner. The row signal steps through 1000, 0100, 0010, and 0001 and then wraps, holding each pattern for a full row period. The later part of the waveform shows the output frozen while enable is low and the jump back to 1000 when reset is asserted mid-scan. All tests pass with no errors.


Top module testbench




Figure 6: A screenshot of a QuestaSim simulation for the top level design


Figure 4 shows the Questa simulation of the lab2_az top level module. The pnp signal alternates between 01 and 10 while seg swaps between the two decoded digits in lockstep, confirming that the shared segment bus only ever presents the digit whose anode is enabled. Lower in the waveform, led follows ~col as the scan walks across the rows with three keys held down. All tests pass with no errors.



Hardware
The design met all of the intended design objectives. On hardware, both digits were stepped through all 16 values independently to confirm that each display follows its own DIP switch, and the keypad was checked key by key to confirm that each press blinks the LED for its column. The brightness of a digit does not change with the number of segments lit, there is no visible bleeding between the two digits, and neither digit flickers. Because the row drivers are open-collector, pressing two keys in the same column does not short two row drivers together, and the scanning signal keeps working correctly with at least two keys held at once.



Figure 7: Picture of the dual seven-segment display showing two independent hexadecimal digits


As shown in Figure 7, switch 1 inputted a hex pattern of 3, switch 2 inputted a hex pattern of C, and the dual seven-segment display correctly displays both.


Keypad scanning on hardware




Figure 8: Picture of the LEDs responding to a keypress on the keypad


As shown in Figure 8, row 3 column 3 is depressed, and LED 3 correctly lights up.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display and Keypad Scanning
text:
Conclusion
The design successfully drove two independent hexadecimal digits on a dual common-anode display from a single time-multiplexed seven-segment decoder, and successfully scanned a matrix keypad so that any keypress blinks the LED for its column. The most interesting part of the lab was that both of the hard problems were solved outside the HDL: the anode current and the multiple-keypress short each needed a transistor.
I spent a total of 20 hours working on this lab.

With over three months of no-contact with SystemVerilog my skills have became a little rusty. Although this lab was a little bit bumpy at first due to all the Radiant issues, I was able to ramp back up pretty fast and got the 7-segment display working in one try. Plus, Quarto is pretty cool! Never have I typed so much Markdown at once, not even during my annoying Amazon internal tool development over the summer.
